claims.text: The starting material is polished, solution-annealed or as-cast CoCrFeNi.
Laser microtexturing will form periodic surface arrays with tens-of-micrometers spacing and several-micrometers depth.
Laser-generated microtextures will promote formation of a self-adaptive, stable oxide tribofilm on CoCrFeNi.
Microtextured dimples or channels will trap wear debris.
Retaining an oxide tribofilm can reduce wear by limiting damaging contact.
Directing debris into microtextured recesses will reduce abrasive contact.
The relevant wear mechanism changes with temperature, with abrasive wear important at lower temperatures and oxidative or adhesive wear important at 600–800 °C.
Oxide films may crack or be broken through under prolonged tribological loading and deformation.
Microtexturing will keep the coefficient of friction at or below that of untextured CoCrFeNi throughout 25–800 °C.
Microtexturing will reduce the CoCrFeNi wear rate by at least 20% relative to the untextured baseline throughout 25–800 °C.
The microtexturing intervention will remain effective in ambient air up to 800 °C and at normal loads up to 10 N.
Applicability of the intervention in corrosive or vacuum environments is unverified.
Humidity and oxidation conditions may affect oxide-film stability.
High-temperature microstructural changes could degrade tribofilm formation or adhesion.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says microtexturing consistently reduces friction, whereas the predicted outcome permits friction merely equal to the untextured baseline.
The predicted outcome permits a coefficient of friction equal to baseline, but the falsification rule requires it to be consistently lower.
